newsitem.title: USA: Consumer debt rise not sustainable - Fed's Lindsey.
newsitem.headline: Consumer debt rise not sustainable - Fed's Lindsey.

text.p: Federal Reserve Gov. Lawrence Lindsey on Thursday expressed concern about an expansion in consumer debt, saying the trend was not sustainable.

Speaking to a conference held by the Consumer Federation of America, Lindsey said some of the increase in debt reflected positive developments in the economy such as the extended period of economic growth and low interest rates.
"When one looks at the data, however, this expansion does raise some troubling statistics," he said, pointing to a trend in which consumers' spending has been outpacing their incomes.
"Roughly for every extra $1 we're earning, we're spending $1.10," Lindsey said. "This is not a sustainable trend."
Noting the extent to which consumer credit has become much more widely available, Lindsey said that has helped to raise living standards by removing liquidity constraints faced by households.

Still, he said some problems were also arising from the situation. "We are seeing for example -- because of extensions of credit to people who may not have had experience before and levels of credit that are unprecedented -- a rise in the number of bankruptcies."
He added, "In the period ahead, I think that high and perhaps rising levels of consumer debt will actually cause the bankruptcy rate to rise further."
Looking at what the trends mean for the economy, Lindsey played down concerns about a threat to the banking sector, saying that those institutions were "quite healthy."
He also predicted that increases in loan losses due to consumer debt expansion would force a reconsideration of lending policies.
The Fed official said that serious economic problems can be avoided as long as there is moderation in the responses of consumers and banks to rising default and deliquency rates.
Regarding consumer debt burdens, Lindsey said that debt-service levels were at record levels if one takes into account automobile leases, which he said were effectively a form of loan.
"I do think we should be aware that we are at new highs and that this may cause some trouble for a large number of households in the future," he said.
Looking ahead, Lindsey said income and spending trends would be favorable for getting through the consumer debt expansion.
"We'll see probably a modest rise in real income in the months ahead and a modest decline the rate of growth of consumption," he predicted.
